summary: DNS is defined across dozens of RFCs, and its terminology has shifted over decades. This document gives current definitions for many DNS terms in one place. It updates RFC 2308 by clarifying "forwarder" and "QNAME", and it replaces RFC 8499 with added terms and clarifications.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the dictionary of internet phone-book words. It says what each term means so people don't talk past each other.

questions: what is the difference between a recursive resolver and a stub resolver
what does qname mean in dns
subtitle: One place to look up what DNS terms mean today, from labels and zones to resolvers and DNSSEC states.

tldr.problem: The DNS is defined across dozens of RFCs, and many of its terms have drifted from their original meanings or were never defined precisely.
tldr.mechanism: The document collects current definitions in one place, grouped by topic (names, response codes, resource records, servers, zones, wildcards, registration, DNSSEC). It quotes the source RFC where the consensus matches and gives a new stand-alone definition where it does not.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice that obsoletes RFC 8499 and updates RFC 2308 by clarifying 'forwarder' and 'QNAME'. It is a reference to skip around in, not a tutorial.

today: RFC 9499 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 219). It obsoletes RFC 8499 and updates RFC 2308 by clarifying the definitions of forwarder and QNAME. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why a DNS Dictionary Exists
sections.content:
The Domain Name System is a simple query-response protocol whose messages in both directions have the same format. The protocol and message format come from RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, and later documents defined more terms. Some terms from those two RFCs now mean something a little different than they did in 1987.

This document contains a wide variety of DNS terms, organized loosely by topic. Some were precisely defined before, some loosely, and some never. Where the community consensus matches an earlier RFC, that RFC is quoted. Where it has shifted, the RFC is mentioned and a new stand-alone definition is given. It is a small revision of RFC 8499, which was itself a substantial revision of RFC 7719.

The RFC warns that someone new to the DNS probably cannot learn it from front to back here. Skipping around, and using the index, is the intended way to read it. The words 'byte' and 'octet' are used interchangeably.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a word book for DNS. You look up a word when you need it instead of reading it like a story.

sections.title: Names, Labels and the Global DNS
sections.content:
A domain name is an ordered list of one or more labels, and a label is an ordered list of zero or more octets. The RFC defines the global DNS using a short list of facets of any naming system: how names are composed, their format, who administers them, what data they carry, what metadata they have, which protocol fetches the data, and the context for resolving them. The private DNS uses the same protocol but does not rely on the global DNS root zone.

In the global DNS each label is between 0 and 63 octets long. In a fully qualified name the last label is the zero-length root label, and the whole name has a maximum length of 255 octets in wire format. Names appear in three formats: wire format (labels each preceded by a length octet), presentation format (labels separated by dots, with the trailing root dot, as in example.tld.), and common display format (the same but with the root dot usually left off).

The section also untangles several loose terms. A fully qualified domain name is often written without the terminating dot. Host name is not defined in the core DNS RFCs and usually means a name following the preferred name syntax. A top-level domain is a zone one layer below the root, such as com or jp, and the RFC says there is nothing special about TLDs from the point of view of the DNS. Other entries cover multicast DNS, locally served zones, subdomains, aliases and the canonical name.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain name is like an address written from the smallest part to the biggest, such as room, building, street. Each part is a label, and the very last empty part stands for the whole world.

sections.title: Response Codes, QNAME and Referrals
sections.content:
Several response codes from RFC 1035 have shorthand names: NOERROR, FORMERR, SERVFAIL, NXDOMAIN, NOTIMP and REFUSED. NODATA is a pseudo response code: the name is valid but there are no records of the requested type, shown by NOERROR with no relevant answers. The RFC notes that calling it NXRRSET is a mistake, since that is a specific error code in RFC 2136.

The header of a DNS message is its first 12 octets. The term QNAME had two meanings: the name in the Question section of a query, or, in RFC 2308, the name in the answer after following any CNAME chain. To remove the confusion the RFC distinguishes QNAME (original), QNAME (effective) and QNAME (final), and notes that in general use QNAME almost always means the original one.

A referral is a response in which a server that is not completely authoritative points the resolver to another place to send its query. A downward referral (from a server authoritative for part of the QNAME) is what normal operation needs to find names beneath a delegation. An upward referral, usually pointing at the root, is never required, and some people regard it as a misconfiguration. A response with only a referral has an empty Answer section, the NS RRset in the Authority section, and the AA bit clear.
sections.plainLanguage: When you ask the wrong office a question, they either say 'no such person here', 'I do not do that kind of thing', or 'ask the office down the hall'. That last one is a referral.

sections.title: Resource Records, RRsets and TTL
sections.content:
An RR is a resource record. An RRset is a set of records with the same owner name, class and type but different data. RFC 2181 requires the TTLs of all records in an RRset to be the same. RRSIG records are the exception to the RRset definition: they are tied to the RRset they sign and do not form RRsets themselves.

The TTL is the maximum time a record may be cached. It is an unsigned number with a minimum of 0 and a maximum of 2147483647, encoded in the less significant 31 bits of the 32-bit field. It is a maximum because a cache operator may shorten it, for example under a policy against large values. The RFC also notes that some servers are known to ignore TTLs on some RRsets, against the advice in RFC 1035.

Other entries define master file (zone file) and presentation format, EDNS (which allows message sizes larger than the original 512-octet limit, a bigger response code space and extra options), the OPT pseudo-record, the SOA field names (MNAME, RNAME, SERIAL, REFRESH, RETRY, EXPIRE, MINIMUM), and address records (types A and AAAA).
sections.plainLanguage: A record is one line in a phone book. A set is all the lines for one name and kind of entry. The time-to-live is a sticker saying throw this copy away after a while because it may be out of date.

sections.title: Resolvers, Servers and Transports
sections.content:
Terms such as 'DNS server' and 'name server' have no formal definition and need context. A resolver extracts information from name servers on behalf of clients. A stub resolver cannot perform all resolution itself and depends on a recursive resolver, which acts in recursive mode: it answers from its cache or queries other servers for the final answer. A recursive query has the RD bit set to 1; a non-recursive query has it set to 0. In iterative resolution the client repeatedly makes non-recursive queries and follows referrals.

An authoritative server knows the content of a zone from local knowledge and answers with the AA flag set. The primary and secondary roles describe which server is the source of zone transfers (AXFR copies the full zone, IXFR only the changes); the RFC notes that current usage has moved from 'master' and 'slave' to 'primary' and 'secondary'. A forwarder is a server used to resolve queries instead of directly using the authoritative nameserver chain, and in current use forwarders often sit between stub resolvers and recursive servers. Priming is the act of finding the list of root servers from a configuration, and root hints is the file used for it.

The section also defines policy-implementing and open resolvers, split DNS and views, passive DNS, anycast, and the transports: Classic DNS (UDP or TCP, unencrypted), DNS-over-TLS, DNS-over-HTTPS and DNS-over-QUIC, plus XFR-over-TLS for zone transfers.
sections.plainLanguage: Your computer asks a helper, the helper asks the big offices one after another, and at the end an office that really owns the answer replies. Different helpers have different jobs, and this part gives each a name.

sections.title: Zones, Delegation and Registration
sections.content:
A zone is a unit of authoritative information. The apex (or origin) is the name at the top of a zone, and a zone cut separates a parent zone from a child zone. Delegation happens when an NS RRset is added in the parent zone for the child origin. Glue records are address records for name servers that are only needed when the server's name is below the cut, so that the NS records do not send you to the very address you are trying to learn.

Following RFC 9471, the relationship between the NS owner name, the name server name and the zone origin is one of three types: unrelated, in-domain, or sibling domain. The RFC gives a table, for example example.org with ns.example.org as in-domain and ns.ietf.org as sibling domain. The terms lame delegation and bailiwick are described as drifted or confusing and are to be considered historic.

Wildcards (records owned by a name starting with the asterisk label) are treated in their own section, including terms like closest encloser and source of synthesis. The registration model defines registry, registrant, registrar, EPP, WHOIS, RDAP, DNS operator and public suffix, noting that who decides what goes in a zone is its registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a company handing a department to a manager and writing down who to ask for that department. The handover is a delegation, and the note with the manager's phone number, when needed, is glue.

sections.title: DNSSEC Terms and States
sections.content:
Most DNSSEC terms come from RFCs 4033, 4034, 4035 and 5155, and this document highlights those that caused confusion. A signed zone has signed RRsets and properly built DNSKEY, RRSIG, NSEC (or NSEC3) and optionally DS records. NSEC and NSEC3 provide authenticated denial of existence, and NSEC3 mitigates zone enumeration and supports Opt-Out. Validation can mean checking signatures, checking responses such as denial of existence, or building an authentication chain from a trust anchor to a response.

The key terms are key signing key (signs only the apex DNSKEY RRset), zone signing key (signs the other RRsets) and combined signing key. The RFC stresses that operational practice, not protocol, decides which role a key plays, and that the SEP flag is only a hint.

A validating resolver can place a response in one of four states, defined in RFC 4033 and RFC 4035. This document quotes both definitions and takes no position on reconciling them.
sections.plainLanguage: DNSSEC is a wax seal on the answers. This part names the seals and the keys, and says what a checker should do when a seal is good, missing or broken.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The security section is one sentence: these definitions do not change any security considerations for either the global DNS or private DNS. The IANA section records that references to RFC 8499 in the IANA registries have been replaced with references to this document.

Because the document only defines words, the practical risk is misunderstanding rather than a new attack. Using the agreed meanings, for example for 'validating resolver' or 'lame delegation', is how the community avoids talking past each other.
sections.plainLanguage: A dictionary does not open any new doors for burglars. It just makes sure everyone means the same thing by each word.

viz.caption: DELEGATION TYPES FROM TABLE 1 OF THE RFC (SELECTED ROWS)
THE FOUR DNSSEC STATES A VALIDATING RESOLVER CAN REACH

items.title: Secure
items.text: A trust anchor and chain of trust exist, and the signatures verify.

items.title: Insecure
items.text: No chain of signed DNSKEY and DS records to the data, for example in an unsigned zone.

items.title: Bogus
items.text: A chain should exist but signatures fail or expected data is missing.

items.title: Indeterminate
items.text: No trust anchor says that part of the tree should be secure.
